name: Greece
tagline: The birthplace of Western civilization's founding myths and monuments, spread across a mainland and thousands of islands where ancient ruins, Byzantine monasteries and whitewashed villages sit within a single, well-connected country.
cardDescription: The Acropolis and Santorini's caldera, Crete's beaches and Meteora's cliff-top monasteries, island-hopping and ancient history in one country.
metaDescription: A complete Greece travel guide: the 10 best places to visit, ferries and flights, island-hopping, food, costs, etiquette and a two-week itinerary.

image.alt: Santorini's whitewashed villages above the volcanic caldera at sunset

intro: Greece holds a disproportionate share of the ideas and monuments that shaped Western civilization — democracy, philosophy, theatre and the Olympic Games all trace directly back here, and the country's ancient sites remain standing, walkable and central to a visit rather than curated behind glass alone. The Acropolis, Delphi and Olympia are not just ruins but the actual physical settings where these ideas took shape.

That ancient inheritance sits alongside a different Greece scattered across more than 200 inhabited islands, each with its own distinct character — Santorini's volcanic caldera views, Mykonos' nightlife, Crete's scale and Corfu's Venetian-influenced architecture all coexist within ferry or short-flight reach of each other and the mainland.

The practical spine connecting all of this is a well-developed network of ferries and short domestic flights, alongside a food and hospitality culture — genuine philoxenia, the traditional obligation of welcoming strangers — that consistently exceeds what visitors expect even after reading about Greek hospitality in advance.
placesIntro: Ordered roughly by how strongly we would recommend each for a first visit — though Meteora, Nafplio and Thessaloniki reward a second trip just as much as a first.
thingsToDoIntro: The experiences that recur across the country and that make a Greece trip feel like more than a checklist of ruins and beaches.

thingsToDo.title: Island-hop by ferry

image.alt: A ferry in Piraeus harbour, the main gateway to the Greek islands

thingsToDo.text: Greece's ferry network makes combining several islands in one trip straightforward, from high-speed catamarans to slower, more scenic conventional ferries.
thingsToDo.tip: Book high-speed ferries ahead in peak summer season, when popular routes between the Cyclades islands can sell out.

thingsToDo.title: Eat a proper taverna meal

image.alt: Outdoor seating at a traditional Greek taverna

thingsToDo.text: A long, unhurried meal of shared mezze plates, grilled fish or meat and local wine, eaten at a genuine neighbourhood taverna rather than a tourist-strip restaurant.
thingsToDo.tip: A taverna filled with Greek families rather than tour groups is a reliable sign of quality and fair pricing.

thingsToDo.title: Watch the sunset from a caldera or hilltop

image.file: File:View of Caldera at Sunset from Imerovigli, Santorini.jpg
image.alt: Sunset over Santorini's caldera, seen from Imerovigli

thingsToDo.text: Santorini's caldera is the most famous version, but spectacular sunset viewpoints exist across the islands and mainland alike.
thingsToDo.tip: Arrive at least 30 minutes ahead of sunset at Santorini's most famous viewpoints, which fill with crowds well before the sun actually sets.

thingsToDo.title: Visit an ancient site with real context

image.alt: The Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens

thingsToDo.text: Hiring a local guide or reading ahead transforms a visit to the Acropolis, Delphi or Olympia from a photo stop into something considerably more meaningful.
thingsToDo.tip: Visit major ancient sites at opening time in summer, both for the light and to beat the heat and the crowds.

thingsToDo.title: Swim in clear water

image.file: File:ELA - Clear shallow water at Elafonisi Beach, Crete, Greece, 2015.jpg
image.alt: Clear shallow water at Elafonisi Beach, Crete

thingsToDo.text: Greece's beaches and coves offer some of the Mediterranean's clearest, bluest water, from organised beach clubs to quiet, undeveloped coves reachable only by boat or a short hike.
thingsToDo.tip: Sperlonga-style beach umbrella rental fees are common at organised beaches — bring your own gear if you'd rather avoid the charge.

thingsToDo.title: Try a Greek coffee or ouzo, properly

image.alt: A bottle of ouzo, Greece's anise-flavoured spirit

thingsToDo.text: Greek coffee, brewed slowly and served with the grounds settled at the bottom, and ouzo, sipped slowly with water and mezze, are both genuine social rituals rather than quick drinks.
thingsToDo.tip: Order Greek coffee 'metrio' for medium sweetness if you don't have a strong preference — it's the most commonly served default.

foodIntro: Greek food's international reputation as gyros and Greek salad undersells it badly. Genuine regional variety, fresh seafood and a deep olive oil and wine culture make the case on their own.

foods.name: Moussaka

image.alt: Moussaka, layered aubergine, spiced meat and béchamel

foods.text: Layered aubergine, spiced minced meat and a genuine béchamel top, a defining Greek comfort dish found on menus nationwide with real regional variation.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional tavernas across the country, ideally made fresh rather than reheated from a steam tray.

foods.name: Souvlaki and gyros

image.file: File:Say Souvlaki - chicken gyros wrap - 21 June 2026.jpg
image.alt: A chicken gyros wrap, Greece's beloved everyday fast food

foods.text: Grilled skewered meat or a rotisserie wrap, Greece's most beloved everyday fast food, eaten standing up from a paper wrap or on a plate with fries.
foods.whereToTry: Dedicated souvlaki shops nationwide — a queue of locals is a reliable sign of quality.

foods.name: Fresh Greek seafood

image.alt: Grilled octopus, a classic Greek seafood dish

foods.text: Grilled octopus, whole fish and shellfish, excellent around the islands and coastal towns, typically priced by weight.
foods.whereToTry: Harbourside tavernas in fishing towns, where the day's catch is often on genuine display.

foods.name: Greek salad (horiatiki)

image.alt: Horiatiki, a traditional Greek salad with feta

foods.text: Tomatoes, cucumber, olives and a genuine slab of feta, dressed simply in olive oil, a dish that tastes considerably better in Greece than its export version ever suggests.
foods.whereToTry: Any taverna nationwide, though tomato quality peaks in summer.

foods.name: Greek wine

image.file: File:Glass of wine at Manali Winery, Sikinos.jpg
image.alt: A glass of wine at a Greek island winery

foods.text: A winemaking tradition dating back millennia, with distinct regional grape varieties like Assyrtiko from Santorini increasingly recognised internationally.
foods.whereToTry: Island and mainland wineries offering tastings, and any taverna's house wine, often a good value option.

foods.name: Baklava and Greek sweets

image.alt: Baklava, a honey-soaked filo pastry dessert

foods.text: Honey-soaked filo pastry desserts, alongside loukoumades (honey doughnuts) and other rich, syrup-soaked sweets shaped by centuries of Ottoman and Byzantine influence.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional zaharoplasteio (sweet shops) nationwide, particularly strong in Thessaloniki.

foods.name: Olive oil, seriously

image.alt: A bottle of extra virgin Cretan olive oil

foods.text: Greece is among the world's largest olive oil producers, and the genuine quality difference between a proper Greek olive oil and an export supermarket bottle is considerable.
foods.whereToTry: Family-run producers across the Peloponnese and Crete, several offering tastings and direct sales.

practicalIntro: The essentials, current for 2026. Greece is straightforward and well organised to travel in, with ferry timing and August crowds the two practicalities that most often catch visitors out.

practical.language: Greek nationally, with widespread English ability in tourist areas, hotels and restaurants across the mainland and islands.
practical.money: Card payment is widely accepted in cities and tourist areas, though small island tavernas, kiosks and taxis sometimes remain cash-preferring. Carry some cash as a backup, especially on smaller islands.
practical.visa: Visa-free entry for up to 90 days within a 180-day period for many nationalities including the US, Canada, Australia and UK, under the Schengen Area's common rules.
practical.plugs: Type C and F (Europlug/Schuko), 230 V, 50 Hz — standard continental European two-pin plugs.
practical.tipping: Not obligatory but appreciated. Rounding up or adding roughly 5–10% for good restaurant service is standard practice.
practical.safety: Very safe overall, with low rates of violent crime against visitors. Pickpocketing occurs in crowded tourist areas and on public transport in Athens — standard vigilance is enough to avoid it.
practical.connectivity: Good 4G and 5G in cities and larger islands, though coverage can thin out on smaller islands and in mountain areas. A local SIM or eSIM is worth arranging on arrival.
practical.timeZone: Eastern European Time (UTC+2) in winter, Eastern European Summer Time (UTC+3) from late March to late October.

budget.label: Backpacker
budget.value: €50–80 per day — hostels, taverna lunches, ferry deck class

budget.label: Mid-range
budget.value: €100–170 per day — three-star hotels, restaurant meals, ferry cabins

budget.label: Comfortable
budget.value: €190–320 per day — good hotels, guided tours, domestic flights

budget.label: Santorini and Mykonos supplement
budget.value: Add roughly 25–40% to any budget band specifically on these two islands

bestTime.headline: May–June and September
bestTime.summary: Greece's summer heat and crowds peak hard in July and August, and late spring and early autumn offer the best balance of warm weather, open facilities and manageable crowds.

seasons.text: Mild, increasingly warm weather with wildflowers across the countryside and crowds well below the July-August peak.
Hot, dry and the most reliable weather for swimming, but also the most crowded and expensive months, especially on the islands.
Warm sea temperatures lingering from summer, comfortable air temperatures and noticeably thinner crowds than August.
Mild on the mainland but quiet on the islands, where many hotels, restaurants and ferry routes reduce service or close entirely.

bestTime.avoid: Mid-August without accommodation and ferry tickets booked far ahead — the Greek domestic August holiday period pushes the islands to their busiest, most expensive point of the year.

tripDuration.headline: 10–14 days for a first trip
tripDuration.summary: Greece's ferry and flight network makes an ambitious island-and-mainland itinerary workable, though the Cyclades and Crete each reward more time than a rushed loop allows.

options.text: Athens alone fills four or five days, or Athens plus a single island like Santorini or Mykonos reached by short flight or ferry.
options.detail: A short Greece trip is better spent deeply in one or two places than spread thin across the islands.

options.text: Athens, then island-hop between Santorini and Mykonos — the classic first-trip route connecting ancient history and the Cyclades.
options.detail: Add a day in Delphi for a well-rounded route without extending the core itinerary much.

options.text: The itinerary on this page: Athens, Delphi, Meteora, then island-hopping through Santorini, Mykonos and Crete, covering both the mainland's ancient history and the islands' range.
options.detail: Enough time to add Nafplio and the Peloponnese or Thessaloniki to the classic Athens-and-islands route.

options.text: Add Rhodes, Corfu or a slower, multi-week island-hopping route through the Cyclades and Dodecanese.
options.detail: The outer islands and an unhurried ferry-hopping pace are where a second Greece trip belongs.

transport.intro: Greece's ferry network connects the islands in this guide, while domestic flights and a growing rail network cover the mainland.

options.text: Connect [[athens|Athens]]' port of Piraeus to [[santorini|Santorini]], [[mykonos|Mykonos]] and [[crete|Crete]], with high-speed and conventional options on most routes.
options.detail: Book high-speed ferries ahead in July and August, when popular Cyclades routes can sell out days in advance.

options.text: Short flights from Athens reach [[santorini|Santorini]], [[mykonos|Mykonos]], [[crete|Crete]], [[rhodes|Rhodes]] and [[corfu|Corfu]] in under an hour, considerably faster than the ferry alternative.
options.detail: Book budget carrier fares a little ahead for low prices, particularly outside peak summer weekends.

options.text: A comprehensive network connects [[athens|Athens]] to [[delphi|Delphi]], [[meteora|Meteora]], [[nafplio-peloponnese|Nafplio]] and [[thessaloniki|Thessaloniki]] reliably and affordably.
options.detail: Buy tickets a day ahead for popular routes in peak season rather than relying on walk-up availability.

options.text: Useful for exploring [[crete|Crete's]] scale and the wider [[nafplio-peloponnese|Peloponnese]] at a flexible pace beyond the main towns.
options.detail: An International Driving Permit is recommended, and mountain roads can be narrow and winding.

options.text: A clean, efficient system covering central Athens well, including a direct airport line.
options.detail: A combined ticket covers metro, bus and tram within the same fare period.

itinerary.intro: Athens and ancient mainland sites first, then island-hopping through the Cyclades and Crete. Covers six of the ten destinations in this guide.

culture.intro: Greek culture varies between the mainland and the islands, but a handful of broadly shared norms — hospitality, a relaxed relationship with time, and a strong family and community focus — hold nationwide.

etiquette.title: Philoxenia, hospitality to strangers, is taken seriously
etiquette.text: Greeks have a real cultural tradition of welcoming visitors warmly, and hospitality offered is generally meant sincerely rather than as a transaction.

etiquette.title: Time runs more relaxed than in northern Europe
etiquette.text: Greek time ('siga siga', slowly slowly) means schedules and reservations are treated with more flexibility than visitors from punctuality-focused cultures may expect.

etiquette.title: Meals are a genuine social occasion
etiquette.text: Dinner runs late by many countries' standards, often starting after 9pm, and is meant to be lingered over rather than rushed.

etiquette.title: Church and tradition still hold real weight
etiquette.text: Greek Orthodox Christianity shapes daily life, holidays and etiquette even for visitors who aren't religious themselves — dress modestly when visiting churches and monasteries.

etiquette.title: Directness and warmth coexist
etiquette.text: Greeks are often direct in conversation, which is not meant as rudeness — it typically comes paired with real warmth once you get past first impressions.

etiquette.title: August is a genuine national holiday month
etiquette.text: Many Greek businesses close for part of August as owners take their own holidays — this is a real cultural institution, not poor planning.

dos: Dress modestly when visiting churches and monasteries — cover shoulders and knees
Greet with a warm hello and accept hospitality graciously when offered
Linger over meals rather than rushing — it's part of the social occasion
Learn a few basic Greek phrases — the effort is appreciated
Book ferries and island accommodation well ahead for July and August travel
Carry some cash for smaller island tavernas, kiosks and taxis
donts: Don't rush a taverna meal — service is deliberately unhurried, not slow
Don't wear beach clothes into churches or monasteries
Don't assume every small island business takes cards — some remain cash-only
Don't be surprised if some businesses close for part of August
Don't skip travel insurance for ferry-dependent island itineraries — weather can delay crossings
Don't rent a moped without genuine experience and a proper licence — road conditions vary considerably by island

tipsIntro: The things that most often go wrong on a Greece trip, in rough order of how much they cost people.
tips: Book inter-island ferries and flights as early as possible for July and August travel — popular routes sell out.
Build a buffer day into ferry-dependent itineraries — weather can delay or cancel crossings, especially in shoulder season.
Carry some cash — smaller island tavernas, kiosks and taxis can be cash-preferring.
Book Santorini and Mykonos accommodation many months ahead for summer — both islands' rooms fill and prices spike early.
Dress modestly for churches and monasteries — cover shoulders and knees, particularly at Meteora.
Avoid renting a moped without real experience — road conditions and traffic vary considerably by island.
Pack for real heat in July and August, particularly on the Cyclades islands, and plan around the midday sun for sightseeing.
Reserve Acropolis tickets online well ahead in summer, when walk-up queues can mean significant waiting in the heat.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Greece?
faq.a: Ten to fourteen for a first trip. Eight to ten covers Athens and two islands with reasonable pacing; twelve to sixteen lets you add Delphi and Meteora to the classic Athens-and-islands route, which is the itinerary on this page. Four or five days is enough for Athens alone, and Athens alone justifies a trip.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit Greece?
faq.a: May to June and September are the sweet spots — warm weather, manageable crowds and lower prices than peak summer. July and August bring the most reliable sunshine at the cost of genuine crowds and heat; winter is quiet but many island businesses close.

faq.q: Do I need a car in Greece?
faq.a: Only for specific regions. Ferries and flights cover the islands well, and Athens' metro covers the capital. A car becomes useful for exploring Crete's scale and the wider Peloponnese at a flexible pace.

Mid-range travel runs about €100–170 per person per day, with Santorini and Mykonos adding a genuine premium over that figure. Booking ferries and flights well ahead and eating at neighbourhood tavernas rather than tourist-strip restaurants are the biggest levers on cost.

Very. Violent crime against visitors is rare, and most areas are safe to walk in the evening. The practical risk is pickpocketing in crowded tourist areas and on Athens' public transport, manageable with ordinary vigilance around bags and phones.

Book ferries or flights between your chosen islands ahead of time, particularly in summer, and build a buffer day or two into the itinerary in case of weather delays — most visitors combine two to four islands in a single trip rather than attempting more.
